frase_gancho.texto: Silk flowers on velvet and lace that lights up the face.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the flowers of the Isthmus, we move on to the red of the highlands. Look for a long huipil in a deep red, with bands of woven geometric designs and colorful tassels.

guion_corto.texto: This is the formal dress of Zapotec women from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, in Oaxaca. It consists of a short huipil and a full skirt of velvet, or of satin fabric, covered with enormous flowers embroidered by hand with silk thread: roses, tulips, and pansies. The skirt ends in a starched lace ruffle. For the most important festivities, the women put on the resplandor, a white lace headdress that surrounds the face like a halo. Necklaces of gold coins and filigree jewelry complete the outfit. It is clothing made with a great deal of work and a great deal of pride. In the Isthmus, women are known for being strong, and for being the owners of commerce and of the festivities.

guion_largo.texto:
Few outfits in the world draw as much attention as this one. Enormous flowers on dark velvet, gold necklaces, white lace that frames the face like a halo. It is the formal dress of the tehuana, the Zapotec woman of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and it has become one of the most recognizable symbols of Mexico.

First, the context. The Zapotec of the Isthmus call themselves Binnizá, which means “people of the clouds.” And the Zapotec of the valley, the people of Monte Albán, worshipped [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo), the god of rain, as you saw in the Oaxaca Hall downstairs. A people of the clouds, a god of rain: water was always at the center of their way of seeing the world.

Now the embroidery. The flowers on the outfit are embroidered by hand, with silk, on velvet or satin. They are roses, tulips, and pansies, flowers that arrived in Mexico with the Spanish and that here became part of a tradition of their own. It is believed that the taste for these embroidered flowers took hold starting in the nineteenth century, when European fabrics were combined with local talent. The result is enormous: each flower can measure dozens of centimeters.

A legend tells that the resplandor was born from the lace of a baptismal gown, which arrived by sea and which a woman put on her head. Whether or not it is true, the story shows how the Isthmus makes its own everything that arrives. When La Sandunga, the famous song of the Isthmus, plays at a festival, the women dance to it wearing this outfit.

Next, the resplandor. It is a headdress of starched white lace that is worn around the face, as if it were a frame or a sun. It is worn at the most important festivities, such as the velas, which are great community celebrations of the Isthmus with music, dancing, and food. Imagine dozens of women in resplandores dancing together: it must look like a field of suns.

The jewelry tells a story too. The necklaces of gold coins, called ahogadores, and the filigree chains are family heirlooms. In the Isthmus, gold is a form of savings and of pride. A woman who wears her jewelry shows her fortune and that of her lineage.

The tehuana is known for being independent. She is known for running commerce, the markets, and the household economy, and for having a very strong place within the family. That image of a self-assured woman became famous throughout the country. Frida Kahlo, who admired that strength, adopted the tehuana dress as part of her image, and brought it into portraits and photographs that traveled around the world.

In Juchitán and other towns of the Isthmus, the muxes, people whose gender identity has a recognized place in Zapotec culture, also wear this outfit and take part in the velas.

When you see the dress, do not think of a costume. Think of hours of embroidery, of generations of tradition, and of a way of saying “here I am.” The Isthmus of Tehuantepec is a place of winds, of heat, of music, and of festivities, and this clothing is its way of showing it.

texto: Look for the embroidered flowers: how many different colors do they have?
Observe the white lace that forms the resplandor around the face
Notice the gold jewelry and the ruffle on the skirt

texto.Technique/Material: Velvet embroidered by hand with silk, pleated lace, starch and gold metalwork
texto.Function: Gala attire for patron saint vigil festivals, stewardships and celebrations of identity

texto.pregunta: Myth: The tehuana dress is a party costume that nobody wears anymore.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is formal clothing that many women of the Isthmus still wear at the velas and at other festivities. Each embroidery is handwork that takes many hours.
